opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a hard question, and honestly one I still struggle with myself. A lot of students, especially early on, look at very external signals: how many papers did I get into CVPR or NeurIPS this year, how many citations, how many GitHub stars. Those things aren't meaningless, but I think they're lagging indicators at best, and sometimes they're just noise.

What I usually tell my students is to ask a few different questions. First: are you working on something you genuinely find interesting, where you'd keep thinking about it even if nobody was grading you? Because research is a long game, and if you're only driven by the deadline cycle, you burn out, and you also tend to do incremental work that everyone else is doing at the same time.

Second: are you learning to tell what is important? I think that's maybe the single most valuable skill. Execution matters, and in the beginning you should get really good at running experiments, debugging, being careful. But over time the thing that separates people is taste: can you look at the landscape and say, this problem matters, this one doesn't, this direction will look obvious in three years? If you notice your judgment improving, that you can predict which ideas will work, or you're less often fooled by flashy results, that's a very good sign, even if the paper count isn't high yet.

Third, and I think this one is underrated: has your work changed how other people think, even a little? Not necessarily citations, but do people come to you and say, "I tried your idea and it helped," or "that paper made me reconsider something"? Some of the work I'm proudest of wasn't the most hyped at the time, but it slowly became something people built on. That kind of influence is slower, but it's more real.

And finally, I'd say be honest with yourself. Research involves a lot of failure. Most ideas don't work. So "doing well" doesn't mean everything succeeds. It means you're failing in informative ways, asking better questions over time, and becoming someone whose taste and judgment you can trust. If that's happening, I think you're on the right track, regardless of what the short-term metrics say.

r001.rationale: It warns that papers, citations, and other short-term metrics are lagging or noisy signals, and says students are on track regardless of short-term metrics if they are improving over time.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes gradual improvement and influence, but does not clearly frame a researcher’s overall quality as determined by the accumulation of their work over time.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get asked a lot, and I think the honest answer is that most of the obvious signals are misleading.

The easiest thing to measure is paper count, citations, how many acceptances you got at CVPR or NeurIPS this year. And when I was a student, I definitely looked at those numbers. But I've come to believe that if you optimize for them directly, you end up doing a kind of research that's very safe, very incremental. You find a benchmark, you squeeze out one or two points, you write it up. You can be very "productive" that way and still not be a good researcher.

So what I tell my own students is to ask a few different questions instead.

The first one is: do you have taste? Can you look at a problem and tell whether it's the right problem to work on? Can you look at a result and know whether it actually matters, or whether it's just noise that happens to be above the baseline? That's hard to measure, but you can feel it developing. Early on, you basically take whatever your advisor hands you. A couple of years in, you should start disagreeing with your advisor sometimes, and being right some of the time. That's a very good sign.

The second one is: are you learning things you didn't know a year ago? Not just techniques, but ways of thinking. If you look back at your work from twelve months earlier and feel slightly embarrassed, that's actually healthy. If you feel the same as you did a year ago, that's a warning sign, even if the paper count went up.

The third thing, and this is maybe the most important to me, is whether people in the community start to trust your judgment. Not whether they cite you, but whether, when you say "I think this direction is interesting," people take it seriously. That reputation builds slowly and it's based on whether your previous bets turned out to be meaningful. Things like ResNeXt or ConvNeXt, in hindsight, were not about beating a number. They were about asking a question that other people also found worth asking.

And I'd add one more thing: pay attention to whether you still enjoy it. Research is a long game. If the only thing keeping you going is the next deadline, you'll burn out, and you probably won't do your best work anyway. The students I see doing well are the ones who are genuinely curious, who want to understand why something works, not just that it works.

So, to put it simply: don't judge yourself by output. Judge yourself by whether your taste is improving, whether you're changing, and whether your ideas are starting to influence how other people think.

r001.rationale: The response says not to judge yourself by output metrics such as paper counts or acceptances, and points students toward signs that develop over time.

r002.rationale: It says community trust builds slowly based on whether prior research bets proved meaningful, and asks students to assess how their taste, thinking, and influence develop over time.

astra-6.text:
I think students should pay attention to how their judgment is developing. Can you identify an interesting problem and explain why it matters? When an experiment fails, can you learn something from it and decide what to try next? Are you becoming more independent in making those decisions?

Papers and acceptances give you some feedback, but they’re noisy signals. You can do thoughtful work and get rejected, or get a paper accepted without really understanding why something worked. So I would look over a longer period: compared with six months ago, are you asking better questions? Are you more willing to challenge your own assumptions? Can you explain your results more clearly, including what you still don’t understand?

And I’d encourage students to talk with their advisors about those things explicitly. If the only question is, ‘How many papers have I published?’ you miss a lot of what it means to grow as a researcher.

r001.rationale: The response says to assess progress over a longer period and warns that papers and acceptances are noisy signals, discouraging moment-by-moment judgments.

r002.rationale: It recommends looking at development over time, but does not say a researcher’s overall quality is determined by the accumulation of their work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think students should be careful about judging themselves only by external signals—how many papers they publish, whether a paper gets accepted, or how many citations it receives. Those things give you some information, but they’re noisy, especially early on.

A more useful question is: Are you becoming more independent? Can you identify an interesting problem, explain why it matters, and design an experiment that actually helps you understand it? When something fails, can you figure out what you learned and what to try next?

You can ask your advisor and peers for honest feedback, but I would compare yourself mostly with where you were six months or a year ago. Are your questions getting sharper? Is your judgment improving? Are you doing the work because you want to understand something, rather than just finish a paper? If those things are improving, that’s a meaningful sign that you’re growing as a researcher.

r001.rationale: The response says external signals are noisy, especially early on, and recommends comparing progress over six months or a year, which advises against judging research performance at each moment.

r002.rationale: It recommends looking at growth over time, but does not frame a researcher’s overall quality as determined by the accumulated body of their work.
